messages.content: You grade one rewritten spot in a learner's English post before they publish it. You are fair: anything a fluent member of this community would write that says exactly what the writer means passes, however different from the reference.

Where it will be posted: the café's printed autumn menu. Readers: tourists who read English, choosing at the counter.
The writer's note about it, in their words: A translation of this source: 桂花拿铁：用店里自制的桂花糖浆调制，顶上撒一点海盐奶泡。
栗子巴斯克奶酪蛋糕：外表焦香，里面依然软嫩。
无酒精热红酒：加了肉桂、橙皮和丁香，适合阴雨天喝。
Given names and terms: Osmanthus latte, Basque cheesecake.
What the writer means here (confirmed by them): 桂花拿铁：用店里自制的桂花糖浆调制，顶上撒一点海盐奶泡。
The part they are rewriting was: "milk cap"
What was wrong with it, which the new version must fix: Readers expect a café topping to be called foam, cream or froth. 'Milk cap' is not a standard coffee term, and in English it most likely suggests a mushroom, so the topping is not clear.
Reference version: "foam sprinkled on top"
Also fine: "foam on top"; "frothy topping on top"
Likely mistakes, numbered:
1. The topping word is 'cap', 'top', 'hat' or another word that does not name a coffee foam.
2. The salt is not shown as sitting on top, or the action of adding it is missing.
3. Sea salt and milk are stacked as if the milk itself is salty, e.g. 'sea salt milk', which a fluent writer would not use.
Choices in the reference, numbered, each with the reason the tutor gave for it:
1. foam: Cafés call this topping foam, not cap or cream. 'Milk cap' suggests a mushroom to readers. A learner might write 'milk cap' or 'milk top', which neither matches the drink.
2. sprinkled: The source's 撒 means the salt is scattered lightly over the top, not poured or stirred in. 'Sprinkled' keeps that light, scattered sense that 'with ... on top' alone loses.
3. on top: Keep the position in the same phrase as the verb so it reads as one topping, not a separate clause. The sentence already says 'with a little sea salt', so 'on top' completes the picture.
The learner's new version: "foam sprinkled on top"
The post with it in place:
<<<
Osmanthus latte: house-made osmanthus sauce, with a little sea salt foam sprinkled on top.
Chestnut Basque cheesecake: the outside is baked a bit burnt, inside still soft.
Hot red wine (alcohol-free): cinnamon, orange peel and cloves, suitable for rainy days.
>>>

Rules:
- verdict "pass" when a fluent reader would take away the writer's meaning (nothing missing, nothing added that changes it) and nothing in the new version is wrong or unnatural enough that a careful native editor would change it. Matters of taste are not errors. Otherwise "retry".
- A tense that does not fit the surrounding post (present in a past narrative, or the reverse) is an error.
- A word that says something other than what the writer means is an error even when it is fluent (a near-synonym with another sense, a pronoun whose referent becomes unclear).
- Sentence-final punctuation is placed automatically when the version goes into the post: whether the learner typed a full stop (or other final mark) at the very end is never an error and never a reason to retry.
- errors: only real English errors in the new version (grammar, wrong word, a structure carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China)), each with the exact words, the fix, and why (the why always in English). Not differences from the reference.
- The writer's voice stays: casual spelling and capitalisation (all lowercase, capitals for emphasis, keysmashes, stretched letters, a missing apostrophe in a contraction), slang, emoji and the community's own shorthand, wherever fluent members of this community write that way too; so does a greeting or a word from another language used as flavour that readers will get. Names (characters, people, usernames, places, the community's terms) are the writer's: leave how they spell and capitalise them and which name they use, unless a reader could not tell who is meant. None of these is a problem in either pass. But wording carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) (a calque, a collocation, structure or set phrase a fluent writer would not produce) is not voice: it is a problem however casual the post. Never count those as errors.
- check: the number of the most important likely mistake the new version makes, or null.
- other: when something is missing or wrong and no numbered mistake fits, describe the problem: problem (English), reader (optional, one English line in character, only when the meaning suffers), hint (English: points at the gap without giving the words), tell (English: the fix plainly). Else null.
- ticks: numbers of the reference's choices the new version also makes, or makes an equally good equivalent of.
- own: when the learner made a good choice of their own that differs from the reference, one English sentence saying why it works; else null.
- choices: one entry per numbered choice of the reference, in order: n; mine: the learner's exact words doing the same job, or null if their version does not do it; verdict: "same" (they made this choice, or one no reader would tell apart: two coordinated words in another order, an article, a contraction, a synonym with no difference here), "also" (a different choice that is just as right here), "needed" (a different choice, and the reference's is needed). The tutor's reasons are claims, not facts: "needed" only when the reason really holds for their words; when it does not (their words are not wrong or unnatural here), the verdict is "also", "missing" (their version does not do this job); note: only for "also" and "needed", in English, one or two sentences on what their words say or imply here next to the reference's, so they see exactly how the two differ (for "needed", why the reference's choice is needed). Do not repeat the reason the tutor gave; add only what is about their words. When the reason criticised words they kept and it does not hold, the note says so plainly.
- extra: other places where their version differs from the reference in a way worth a word and no numbered choice covers it (at most two): mine, ref (the reference's words for the same job), ok, note (English, as above). Never a difference no reader would notice. [] if none.
- tutor: null when nothing above is a problem. Otherwise what the tutor says to the learner now, in English, addressing them informally, at most two sentences: quote their exact words that need work and say concretely what a reader takes from them versus what they mean (or what is missing, naming the idea, not the English words). This is try number 1: point at the problem without giving the replacement words. Never repeat what the tutor already said to them; never generic advice like "check your meaning".
- repaired: null when nothing above is a problem. Otherwise their version with the smallest changes that fix every problem above: keep their words, word order and structure wherever they work; add what is missing in the same style. It covers exactly the stretch their version covers: never copy in text from the post before or after it.
- The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in English.

First write reads_as: in English, what a reader takes this new version to say, as they would understand it in the post.
Then missing: the parts of the writer's meaning, or of what the original part said and the reference keeps, that the new version leaves out (short English phrases; [] if none). Count meaning, not words: dropping a word that does not change what a reader takes away is fine. If the original's problem was that something was only implied, it is still missing while it is only implied.
Then hits: for each numbered likely mistake, in order, true if the new version makes it.
Then errors, other, choices, extra, tutor and repaired as above; there is no verdict field and no ticks field.

Reply with JSON only, fields in this order: {"reads_as":"","missing":[],"hits":[false,false,false],"meaning_ok":true,"errors":[{"words":"","fix":"","why":""}],"check":null,"other":null,"choices":[{"n":1,"mine":null,"verdict":"same","note":null},{"n":2,"mine":null,"verdict":"same","note":null},{"n":3,"mine":null,"verdict":"same","note":null}],"extra":[],"tutor":null,"repaired":null}
Each extra item, if any, is {"mine":"","ref":"","ok":true,"note":""}.

result.text: {"reads_as":"Osmanthus latte made with house-made osmanthus sauce, topped with a little sea salt foam that is sprinkled on top.","missing":[],"hits":[false,false,false],"meaning_ok":true,"errors":[],"check":null,"other":null,"choices":[{"n":1,"mine":"foam","verdict":"same","note":null},{"n":2,"mine":"sprinkled","verdict":"same","note":null},{"n":3,"mine":"on top","verdict":"same","note":null}],"extra":[],"tutor":null,"repaired":null}
